resources.title: tcmll-1a compilation, full.mp4 (Cordelia's TCMLL 1a execution compilation)
resources.author: Cordelia, per the rouxcubing.com link text. She is also one of the four authors of the 'franz + cordelia + tyler + alavaro' TCMLL alg sheet linked next to it. The video itself names no one.
resources.level: advanced (TCMLL extends full CMLL; for solvers who already know the 42 CMLLs)
resources.summary: This is a public Dropbox shared link to one MP4 file, 'tcmll-1a compilation, full.mp4'. It needs no login. The file is 1,690,842,852 bytes and runs 11:12 (671.8 s). Video is H.264 1920x1080 at 29.97 fps; audio is AAC. The faststart MP4 was created on 2025-10-18 with Apple Core Media. I downloaded it once with curl (TLS verified), probed it with ffprobe and sampled frames with ffmpeg. To find every case title, I scanned the bottom of the frame at 2 fps for the white caption text. That gave 42 caption runs, and I read each caption frame. The file was then deleted; the frames are kept. The footage shows only hands executing algorithms on a 3x3, with no alg text, diagrams, slow motion or move overlay. There are two recording sessions: a white table with an aurora Speedcubeshop mat (about 0-260 s) and a wooden table with a dark Speedcubeshop mat. Each case is performed several times. Its name is burned in as a caption when the case starts, about every 15 s. The 42 captions use 8 'shape' groups taken from twisted-corner naming. Each group has subcases named by permutation pattern: Pac-Man 6 (Almost Solved, Left Bar, Right Bar, Left Opp, Right Opp, Diag); Shuriken 3 (RU-gen, Adj Swap, Diag Swap); Stingray 4 (RU-gen, Diag, Close Bar, Line); Gun 6 (RU-gen, Bars, Checkerboard, Front Slash, Back Slash, Diag); Hammer 6 (RU-gen, Back Bar, Front Bar, Left Column, Right Column, Diag); Turtle 6 (RU-gen, Hidden Diagonal, Bars, Checkerboard, Diag Swap, Upper Triangle); Car 4 (RU-gen, Right Column, Perpendicular Bars, Parallel Bars); Spaceship 7 (RU-gen, Checkerboard, Hidden Diagonal, Bars, Bars (DF-safe), Diag Swap, Slash). Every group starts with an 'RU-gen' case. 'Bars (DF-safe)' shows that alternative algs are kept for when DF must not be disturbed. The hub glossary defines TCMLL ('Tic-Tac') as 'an extension of CMLL to solve the top four corners and twist the bottom right corner to the correct orientation'. The video never explains '1a'. It is probably a subset label from the companion alg sheet, such as one twist direction, but that is unverified. The audio is mostly quiet with short peaks (mean -36 dB) and was not transcribed. This is an execution reference, to be watched alongside the TCMLL alg sheet.

resources.title: Conjugated CxLL - Speedsolving Wiki
resources.author: Speedsolving.com wiki contributors (not verifiable; page blocked)
resources.summary: NOT ACCESSIBLE. Cloudflare bot protection blocks the page. curl got HTTP 403 with 'cf-mitigated: challenge'. Playwright stayed on 'Just a moment... Performing security verification' (Ray ID a5201e2f9e23f268). WebFetch also got 403. I did not route around it. Background comes from a web search snippet of this wiki page and from cubinghistory.com/Techniques/Pseudo (HTTP 200, text saved). Conjugated CxLL (CCxLL) solves the last five corners when the second block is a 1x2x2 square with its last corner missing. You orient one corner and place it at UBR above the square, then do an R move. That leaves a 'pseudo' state with four unsolved corners in the U layer. A normal CxLL/CMLL alg solves them relative to the conjugated corner, and an R' undoes the setup. This cuts the 614 algs of L5C down to 42. It was found independently by Michael James Straughan (2012, for his A2 method, using CLL; he also applied it to OLLCP, ELL and CLL+1) and by Joseph Briggs (2017, for his Roux-based '42' method, 'Conjugated CMLL'). Briggs named it CCxLL. Recognition systems exist from Briggs (U/D sticker orientation, then a sticker pattern compared with the bottom corner's right sticker), Jason Wong (three methods) and ATCRM (Straughan + Tim Mosher, 2021). The rouxcubing.com hub lists it under CMLL > Other CMLL, next to L5C/SL5C. A related data point: tao-yu's Alg-Trainer has a '42 (Shadowslice)' set with 672 entries. That is 42 CMLL cases x 4 pre-setups (R, R U, R U', R U2) x 4 post-setups, scrambled with an 'L7E' generator. Shadowslice is the forum name the trainer credits for the 42 method.
drills: From background only: drill the R-conjugated CMLL. Leave the SB last-pair corner unsolved, move a U corner above the DBR square, do R, recognise the pseudo CMLL, execute, then R'

L5C vs Conjugated CMLL: 614 algs vs 42
The 42 method (Roux-based: FB, 1x2x2 SB square, CCMLL, then edges)
History: Straughan (A2, 2012), Briggs (42, 2017); recognition methods

resources.title: Alg Trainer (Tao Yu)
resources.author: Tao Yu (tao-yu on GitHub). The algs come from many authors credited in the page and set names (algdb, Justin Taylor, Jabari Nuruddin, Chad Batten, and others).
resources.level: all levels of alg learners; for Roux, from learning full CMLL to OH CMLL and variant sets
resources.summary: A static JS alg-memorisation trainer. I rendered it with Playwright, selected CMLL, turned on the virtual cube, generated 4 tests, then switched to OH CMLL. I also read the source from a clone of tao-yu/Alg-Trainer (last commit cb95945, 2024-06-14; MIT, 'Copyright (c) 2017-2021 Tao Yu'). The README says the author learned full ZBLL (493 algs) in 58 days with it. The picker lists 63 alg sets, mostly CFOP/ZZ/2x2. The Roux-relevant ones are 'CMLL' (42 cases: O 2, H 4, Pi 6, U 6, T 6, S 6, aS 6, L 6; several algs per case separated by '/') and 'OH CMLL' (42). Roux-variant sets are '42 (Shadowslice)' (672 = 42 CMLL x 4 pre x 4 post R-conjugations) and 'ZBLSE (John McWilliams)'. ZBLSE has 247 M/U-move edge cases grouped by EO pattern (Oriented 8, 6-Flip 9, 2o/2 16, 0/2 9, Arrow F/B 30+30, 4/0 9, 2o/0 16, 2a/0 30, 1/1 F/B 30+30, 2a/2 30). It is scrambled with the ZBLL generator, so it looks like an edges-first step before ZBLL; its scope is not documented. 'L5E' sets (Justin Taylor, 216; L5EP 12; 2-look FR+EO 18) are last-five-edges sets with the FR edge, not core Roux. A session works like this. Pick a set and optionally tick subsets (unticked = whole set). Enter/Tab/Space gives a scramble, and you set up the case on a real cube or use the virtual cube. Space stops the timer and shows the alg(s). Backspace shows the alg without timing, and the arrow keys browse earlier tests. With the virtual cube, the timer stops by itself when the cube is solved and Esc resets the case. Settings: Use Virtual Cube; Hide timer; Show Scramble; Use Real Scrambles; Random AUF; 'Scramble subsequent steps'; Go in order; 'Don't show alg after stopping timer'; Mirror across M / S, each with a Randomize option; Auto-fix algorithm rotation; line style; 3x3/2x2 virtual cube; Giiker i3S/i3SE Bluetooth; user-defined alg set (paste one alg per line, # comments, 'Add currently selected algs'); preorientation; custom colour scheme; editable key bindings (default layout after Ryan Heise). Preorientation is either full colour neutrality (24 orientations) or three boxes: a fixed rotation, then random repeats of two rotations. The defaults are '', 'x2', 'y', i.e. Roux x2/y colour neutrality. The random part shows in green in front of the scramble (e.g. 'x2 y2 x2 B' R' ...'). For CMLL and OH CMLL, 'Scramble subsequent steps' first applies 100 random LSE triggers (M2, M U M, M U M', M U' M, ..., M' U2 M') before the inverse alg. Then obfuscate() re-solves premoves + inverse alg with a two-phase solver, padding to at least 16 moves. So the scramble shows neither the alg nor a solved LSE, and the trainer explains this on scramblingNote.html. A right-hand 'Algset Statistics' panel showed, for CMLL, mean 10.429 STM / 11.690 SQTM (10.833 / 12.262 including AUF) over 42 algs. The times list shows a running mean. The virtual cube is a flat net that toggles to 3D or hidden on click. A mobile.html beta has the same settings. Sample CMLL test: scramble 'L' F' D' F' L' B' R' B' R2 ...', with three algs shown for the case, such as 'L' U R U' L U R' U'.

resources.title: kSim 2 (Rubik's cube simulator and toolkit)
resources.author: Kirjava (Thom; GitHub kirjavascript)
resources.level: intermediate to advanced (simulator with stage scramblers; keyboard-driven)
resources.summary: The site is HTTP-only. The HTTPS version presents a certificate for another host, so curl refused it and verification was not disabled. The agent proxy tunnels only HTTPS, so Playwright could not load http:// directly. I fetched index.html (a 45-byte stub that loads /root.js) and root.js (1.38 MB webpack bundle) with curl. I served them to Playwright through request interception, then picked the CMLL and LSE scramblers and scrambled. I also read the source from a clone of kirjavascript/kSim (React 15 + MobX + three.js; last commit 65ed7bf, 2020-03-15; served build last modified 2020-05-23). The README says 'kSim 2 is a rubik's cube simulator and toolkit' and thanks Lucas Garron, Josef Jelinek (ACube), Shuang Chen (min2phase), Justin Jaffray and Michael Gottlieb. The UI has collapsible panels. Cube: scrambler select, a colour picker per face, 'Set Scramble Orientation'. Display: Classic, Flat or Three view, opacity, zoom, X/Y camera sliders, facelet borders. Solver: ACube in a web worker, with HTM/QTM/STM metric and Slices / All / Optimal checkboxes, showing the ACube state string. Keymap: an editable key-to-moves table, defaulting to the csTimer-style layout i=R, k=R', j=U, f=U', h=M, g=M'. Timer: status, scramble, times with best and current ao5/ao12/ao100. Move History: a rewind slider over your moves, 'Condense moves'. About: 'Clear all data'. State persists in localStorage. Scramblers (min2phase random-state subsets): Random State, CMLL, LSE, LL, OLL, PLL, CLL, ELL, LSLL, 2GLL, ZBLL (+U/T/AS/S/Pi/H), OLLCP (+subsets), Edges Only, Corners Only. CMLL is a random state of the four U corners and the six LSE edges with F2B solved. The six LSE edges are painted grey, so only the corners and blocks show; I confirmed this in the screenshot. LSE is a random-state LSE plus a random AUF and a random M2, so the centres are off half the time. Session flow: Space gives a new scramble (status 'ready'). The first non-rotation move starts the timer. It stops itself when every face shows one colour among its non-grey stickers, so in CMLL mode the solve ends when the corners and AUF are done. Esc resets the cube, and a reset during a running solve records a DNF. Sample CMLL scramble: 'F R' F' L2 B2 R B2 R B2 U' B2 U B2 R2 D B2 D2 R2 L2'.

resources.title: ZBLL trainer next (Roman Strakhov)
resources.author: Roman Strakhov (GitHub Roman-)
resources.level: advanced (ZBLL is a CFOP/ZZ last-layer set). Listed on rouxcubing.com under CMLL trainers as a model trainer UI
resources.summary: The linked URL fails TLS: 'SSL certificate problem: self-signed certificate'. I did not disable verification. The author's repo github.com/Roman-/zbll names https://www.bestsiteever.net/zbll as the site, and commit 4215205 (2025-10-26) changed the TLD from .ru to .net. So I rendered bestsiteever.net/zbll with Playwright (Select view, Hotkeys, Timer view) and read the Vue 3 + Pinia source (last commit e57eaef, 2025-10-26). The older version is Roman-/zbll-trainer (last commit e7bf54e, 2024-11-29). The content is ZBLL: 472 cases, grouped by OLL shape (H 40; L, Pi, S, T, U, aS 72 each), then COLL, then ZBLL. Each case has several algs and precomputed scrambles grouped by length. This is not Roux content and must not go into the app. Its training design is fully reusable for CMLL, EOLR and TCMLL. Selection: click a group picture to select or deselect the group, click its header to expand. Group colour shows state: green = all, yellow = some, white = none. 'start' practises at random; 'recap each case once' runs through every selected case once. Picking: recap mode draws only cases not yet done this round, then falls back to random. Random mode picks the least-practised case 20% of the time and is uniform otherwise. The scramble uses the shortest length common to all selected cases, so length gives nothing away. It is one of several stored algs, re-expressed after a random y rotation, choosing the version with fewer B moves. Timer: hold space (configurable start delay, default 100 ms), release to start, space to stop. Each result card shows the case picture, scramble, setup, the alg list, a 'Selected' toggle, 'Add to starred preset' and a personal note for the case. Deleting a result (e.g. a misscramble) also gives back its recap credit. Presets save named case selections. Hotkeys: Alt+T timer/select, Delete or Alt+Z delete result, Shift+Delete clear session, Alt+S select/deselect current case, Alt+R recap, Alt+A add to starred, arrows/Home/End to move through results. Settings: scramble size, timer size, font and precision, timer update (on, off, seconds only), start delay, top or side pictures, scramble appendix, light/dark and about two dozen Bootstrap themes, 19 UI languages from community translations. Pictures come from sr-puzzlegen, and the page loads Google Analytics.

resources.title: LSE Edge Orientation (Step 4a) flowchart
resources.author: Antonio Kam ('Anto'), rouxl.es (GitHub Pages repo Rouxles/rouxles.github.io)
resources.level: beginner to intermediate (first step after arrow-only intuitive EO)
resources.summary: This is a PNG (1358x677, 186 KB; added to the repo 2020-06-04, Last-Modified 2020-10-16), shown on rouxl.es/lse.html under the collapsible 'EO Flowchart'. I read it directly and from enlarged crops. Its title is 'LSE Edge Orientation (Step 4a)'. There are two mirrored panels, 'Lefty M Moves' (using U) and 'Righty M Moves' (using U'). Each state is a small grey 3D cube with red stickers marking the visible misoriented edges. Arrows show how each state reaches one of two finishing states with a 3-move trigger. In the lefty panel, the 6-flip goes by M' U M' into the 'M' U M' group. Two states use M2'. Two states use M' U M. Two use M' U2 M', including four bad edges on top. Three use M' U M'. The finishing states are the 'arrow' (3 bad on top + DF), solved by M' U M', and a second 4-bad state solved by M U M'. The righty panel repeats the tree with U' (M' U' M, M' U2' M', M' U' M', finishing with M' U' M' and M U' M'). The lse.html page around it calls the flowchart 'optimal MU solutions for each EO case'. It gives an LSE progression: (1) learn the EO flowchart; (2) track the LR edges during EO and force one LR edge to the D layer, to go 4a into 4b without a pause; (3) learn DFDB recognition, for 4b into 4c without a pause; (4) learn EOLR ('Don't avoid misoriented centers'). The same page links a DFDB guide image, an MC DFDB image, EOLR docs (RH and LH M), the EOLRb trainer (old jeremyg.nl address, now enbyne.tech) and an LSE sim (jeremyg.nl/LSEV.htm, now HTTP 503).

resources.title: Bas's EOLR Cheat Sheet
resources.author: Basilio Noris ('Bas', B4silio), dated 04.08.2023, 'Thank you Anto!'
resources.summary: This is a JPEG (4266x7500, 2.9 MB, Last-Modified 2023-08-04) from the 'Bas's Guides and algsheets' section of basilio.dev/cubing. I read it from row and half-row crops; the small print is partly hard to read. It organises EOLR into 9 EO classes named <bad edges on U>/<bad edges on D>: 3/1 (arrow), 2a/2, 4/0, 2o/2, 2o/0, 0/2, 2a/0, 1/1 and 4/2 (6-flip). Each case diagram is a top-face grid with DB drawn above and DF below. A thick outline marks an unoriented edge. Dark red means the L/R edge's sticker is on top or visible; light red means it is on the side or hidden. Under each diagram is the bold opening and a strategy note; the full EOLR solution is in small print above. Examples: 3/1 'Good Arrows' M, M' U' M', M' U' M; 'OK Arrow' U M' U2 M U 'Switch to good'. Four 3/1 'BAD CASES' are handled with 'M' U M' then solve LR'. 2a/2: 'M2 U' Switch to good arrow', 'M' U M' U Stack bad edges and bring down', 'U2 M U2 M' U' Stack bad non-LR edge with LR, keep on bottom'. 4/0: 'M' U2 M' U2 Swap twice', 'M' U2 M U2 Bring to top'. 2o/2: 'Switch and stack', 'M2 U M' U2 M' U2 Turn into 4/0 and solve'. 2o/0: 'M' U M U' Put on top', 'M' U' M U Works in any direction'; one bad case uses the non-MU 'R U R' U' M' U R U' r' Standard OLL'. 0/2: 'Keep on Top and replace', 'Keep corners on sides, then align with UF color'. 2a/0 and 1/1 have keep/bring-to-top/bottom strategies, and several bad cases 'switch to 1/1' or 'switch to OK arrow'. 4/2 (all bad), e.g. 'M' U M U2 M' U' M' U' Bring adjacent and switch to 1/1 case'. Dashed boxes mark bad cases in every class. A footnote says the cases can be mirrored about different axes. In total there are 51 main diagrams (3/1 8, 2a/2 7, 4/0 4, 2o/2 6, 2o/0 6, 0/2 4, 2a/0 7, 1/1 6, 4/2 3) plus small alternates. It is a strategy map, not an exhaustive alg list: it teaches how to steer each EO class into a good arrow or a 1/1 while placing the L/R edges. The site also hosts an Audio Timer (microphone pause detection: look vs turn time, alg splits, split by voice), a Recon Viewer and a CMLL sheet (ALGS-CMLL.jpg, not read).
drills: For each EO class, learn the strategy family (switch to good arrow, stack bad edges, turn into 4/0, switch to 1/1) before memorising full solutions
Recognise the class from bad-edge counts (U/D) plus where the L/R stickers face (visible vs hidden)
Learn the 'bad case' fallbacks (e.g. M' U M' then solve LR) for when EOLR recognition fails
Practise mirrors of each case (the sheet leaves symmetry to the reader)

resources.title: EOLRb trainer (Jade, enbyne.tech)
resources.author: Jade ('JBG', enbyne.tech; formerly jeremyg.nl)
resources.summary: A small static page plus four scripts (lset_base.js, eolr_solver.js, eolrdict9.js, eolr_draw.js, v0.51). I fetched all four and read them, then drove the page with Playwright. In the browser I generated 4 cases, replayed each first listed solution with the default keys and confirmed the 'solved' readout; I did not run any downloaded code outside the browser. I analysed the solution table in Python as data. The model is LSE-only: 6 edges in slots UL, UR, UB, UF, DF, DB (L/R = the UL/UR pieces, X = M-slice pieces, lowercase = misoriented), a U offset and an M-centre offset; moves are U, U', U2, M, M', M2. As coded, the target 'EOLRb' is: every edge oriented and the UL/UR edges solved relative to the corners, so only 4c remains. A looser, unused EOLR check accepts L and R paired in any opposite pair of slots. Cases: L and R are placed at random in any of the six slots. The EO pattern comes from 8 checkboxes: 3LRF-1F (arrow), 1F-1B, 4-0, 0-2, 2LR-2, 2FB-0, 2BL-0, 2BL-2. There is no 6-flip option, and centres are always aligned. Solutions come from a precomputed table of 960 states (8 patterns x 30 L/R placements x 4 U offsets) with 2,720 solutions. All are optimal (equal length within a state), 1 to 5 per state, 3 to 14 STM. Mean optimal length: arrow 7.6, 2BL-2 8.4, 0-2 9.2, 2FB-0 9.4, 1F-1B 9.6, 2BL-0 10.1, 4-0 10.4, 2LR-2 10.7. The scramble is the inverse of the first optimal solution, hidden by default (Ctrl shows it). 'Allow mirrors' swaps M and M'. 'Add random AUF (may give unoptimal solutions)', off by default, adds AUF only where it changes the case: arrow and 1F-1B get any of 4, 4-0 and 0-2 get none, the rest get 0 or 1. Session: Enter gives a new case. You solve it on a flat canvas net (U face from above with the side stickers of U-layer pieces, F face and DF below, B/DB above) by typing moves. Default keys are S=M, D=M', K=U, L=U'; Esc rebinds them, saved in localStorage. Space redoes the same case and Shift shows the solutions. When your moves reach EOLRb, the page shows 'Your solution' in bold with its STM count and lists the optimal ones. Example: scramble 'U' M U M' U M2', you 'M2 U' M U' M' 5 STM', optimal 'M2 U' M U' M' (5STM)'. Other options: Show bottom (DF/DB bottom stickers), Show back, a 6-colour scheme (U,F,D,B,L,R), and 'Orientations': 24 checkboxes for colour on U and colour on F (colour neutrality). It is keyboard-only, with no touch support and no timer or stats. The cubing page describes it as 'Based on the LSETool backend ... practice any EO set for EOLRb, on any colour scheme. Also suitable for just EOLR'. The same author offers LSETool online (optimal LSE/EOLR solver) and two Google Docs: 'EOLR described' (every EOLR case explained, 'Hardly any algs!') and 'OH CMLL'. rouxl.es links the old jeremyg.nl/EOLRb address, which now returns 503.
